extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners; patent practitioners and applicants (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent process/method claims under 35 U.S.C. §101, with particular focus on claims involving transformations, laws of nature, natural principles, and natural correlations. Explains inquiries, relevant factors, and evidentiary burdens for determining whether a claim is an abstract idea, law of nature, or patent-eligible practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether performance of the claimed method results in or otherwise involves a transformation of a particular article
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transformation and reduction of an article ‘to a different state or thing’ is the clue to patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.” An “article” includes a physical object or substance and can include electronic data representing a physical object or substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a transformation exists, the claims are less likely to be drawn to an abstract idea; if not, they are more likely to be so drawn. For data, the data should be more than an abstract value; the nature of the data must be changed to have a different function or be suitable for a different use. Purely mental processes are not considered an eligible transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The particularity or generality of the transformation: more particular transformations weigh in favor of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing, smelting) show processes using chemical substances or physical acts that are sufficiently definite to confine the patent monopoly. A more particular transformation confines the monopoly and favors eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which the recited article is particular (specific identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the recited article is particular; i.e., can be specifically identified (not any and all articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation applied to a generically recited article would weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the transformation (type/extent of change in state or thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the transformation in terms of the type or extent of change in state or thing (e.g., having a different function or use vs. merely changing location).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation that produces a different function or use weighs toward eligibility; a mere change of location weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the article transformed (object/substance vs concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the article transformed, i.e., whether it is an object or substance versus a concept such as a contractual obligation or mental judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transforming an object or substance weighs toward eligibility, whereas transforming a concept or mental judgment weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use (for transformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether its involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use; the extent to which (or how) the transformation imposes meaningful limits on execution of the claimed method steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method (e.g., in a data gathering step or in a field-of-use limitation) would weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether performance of the claimed method involves an application of a law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An application of a law of nature may represent patent-eligible subject matter even without a particular machine or transformation; if an application exists, claims are less likely to be drawn to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim applies a law/natural phenomenon/natural correlation as a limiting element; if so, assess whether the claim includes additional elements that integrate the natural principle into a practical application amounting to significantly more than the principle itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the application (of a law of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The particularity or generality of the application of the law of nature: broad applicability across many fields weighs against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that generically recite an effect of a law of nature or 'claim every mode' of accomplishing that effect (monopolizing a natural force or patenting a scientific fact) weigh against eligibility (e.g., O'Reilly v. Morse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether claimed method recites application of a law of nature solely involving subjective determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed method recites an application of a law of nature solely involving subjective determinations (e.g., ways to think about the law of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of a law of nature to a particular way of thinking about or reacting to it weighs against eligibility; observable and verifiable processes weigh in favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use (for laws of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether its involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use; the extent to which the application imposes meaningful limits on execution of the claimed method steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the claimed method (e.g., a data gathering step or field-of-use limitation) would weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether a general concept is involved in executing the steps of the method
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a general concept (principle, theory, plan, or scheme) is involved in executing the steps of the method: presence can be a clue the claim is drawn to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a general concept is present, evaluate factors such as preemption, abstractness/sweeping scope, whether claim states a problem vs a particular solution, and whether the concept is disembodied or instantiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which use of the concept would preempt its use in other fields
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which use of the concept, as expressed in the method, would preempt its use in other fields (i.e., effective monopoly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that effectively preempt a concept across fields weigh against eligibility (see Bilski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which the claim is abstract and sweeping (covering known and unknown uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the claim is so abstract and sweeping as to cover both known and unknown uses and be performed through any existing or future machinery or without apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly abstract/sweeping claims that cover all modes of accomplishing an effect weigh against eligibility (Gottschalk v. Benson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which the claim would effectively cover all possible solutions to a problem (problem statement vs particular solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the claim would effectively cover all possible solutions to a particular problem; i.e., that the claim is a statement of the problem rather than a description of a particular solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that are a high-level problem statement and claim every possible solution weigh against eligibility; a particular technical solution weighs in favor (Tilghman example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the concept is disembodied or instantiated (implemented in a tangible way)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the concept is disembodied or whether it is instantiated (implemented) in some tangible way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concept that is well-instantiated (e.g., specific machine parts, tangible components) weighs in favor of eligibility; a disembodied concept weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism(s) by which the steps are implemented (observable/verifiable vs subjective/imperceptible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the performance of the process is observable and verifiable rather than subjective or imperceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps that are observable and verifiable weigh in favor of eligibility; subjective or imperceptible steps weigh against eligibility (Tilghman example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of general concepts that tend to indicate abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include basic economic practices/theories (hedging, insurance), basic legal theories (contracts), mathematical concepts (algorithms), mental activity, interpersonal interactions, teaching concepts, human behavior, instructing 'how business should be conducted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of such general concepts in a claim can be a clue the claim is directed to an abstract idea and therefore may be ineligible absent sufficient integration/instantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh the relevant factors; no single factor is determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the factors relevant to the particular patent application should be weighed to determine whether the method is claiming an abstract idea or is limited to a particular practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence or absence of a single factor will not be determinative; examiners must consider and weigh all relevant factors to reach a proper determination whether the claim as a whole is drawn to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: If not merely an abstract idea, proceed to evaluate other statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the factors indicate that the method claim is not merely covering an abstract idea, the claim is eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101 and must be further evaluated under novelty (102), non-obviousness (103), and definiteness/description/enablement (112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 101 is a coarse filter; 102/103/112 typically are the primary tools for evaluating patentability unless the claim is truly abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim is determined to cover an abstract idea, examiner must reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 with clear rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: If factors indicate the method claim is attempting to cover an abstract idea, the examiner will reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 101, providing clear rationale supporting the determination that an abstract idea has been claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must specifically point out the factors relied upon in making the determination so the applicant can make specific arguments in response; the conclusion must be based on the evidence as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO personnel must establish a prima facie case of unpatentability
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel should review the totality of the evidence (specification, claims, relevant prior art) before reaching a conclusion regarding subject matter eligibility; the examiner bears the initial burden of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record suggests it is more likely than not that the claimed invention is a practical application of an abstract idea or falls within an exception, then USPTO personnel should not reject the claim; after identifying reasons, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend or show eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution: review each claim for all statutory requirements in initial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Under principles of compact prosecution, each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review, even if one or more claims are deficient under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry 1: Is the claimed invention a process (act or series of acts)?
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is defined as an act, or a series of acts or steps. Process (method) claims must be drawn to a process for this analysis to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is not directed to a process, this analysis is not applicable (see MPEP §2106 for products).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry 2: Does the claim focus on use of a natural principle?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim focus on use of a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or naturally occurring relation/correlation (a 'natural principle') as a limiting feature of the claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, the procedure is complete (and analyze for abstract ideas under MPEP §2106). If yes, proceed to Inquiry 3. A claim focuses on a natural principle when it recites a correlation used to make a diagnosis or similar limiting element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and examples of a natural principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural principle is the handiwork of nature and occurs without the hand of man (e.g., disinfecting property of sunlight; relationship between blood glucose levels and diabetes; correlations that manifest when a man-made product interacts with a natural substance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples are illustrative, not limiting. A correlation that is a limiting element of the claim triggers the Inquiry 3 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry 3: Practical application and preemption (integrating the natural principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim include additional elements/steps or a combination of elements/steps that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that the natural principle is practically applied and the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. The claim must do more than state a natural correlation plus a general instruction to 'apply it'; at least one additional element must apply, rely on, or use the natural principle in a significant way that imposes meaningful limits and prevents preemption of all practical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional elements must integrate natural principle (not merely appended extrasolution activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements or steps must relate significantly to the natural principle to impose a meaningful limit on claim scope and show practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements that are merely appended extrasolution activity (e.g., recording a diagnosis on a chart) or routine conventional activities do not integrate the principle and are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional steps must be sufficient to ensure claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle (avoid preemption)
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional elements or steps must narrow the claim so that others are not foreclosed from using the natural principle (a basic tool of scientific and technological work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-understood, purely conventional, or field-of-use limitations are insufficient; a claim that confines reach to particular patent-eligible applications (e.g., a new drug or a new way of using a drug) can be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appending conventional steps at a high level of generality does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Appended conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality, to a natural principle do not make the claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level recitations of known steps that add nothing specific to the natural principle will fail Inquiry 3 (see Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity does not add specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps that amount to instructions that are well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by those in the field add nothing specific to the natural principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such steps are insufficient to render the claim patent-eligible under Inquiry 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that cover known and unknown uses that can be performed by any machinery (or none) lack sufficient features
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers known and unknown uses of a natural principle and can be performed through any existing or future-devised machinery, or even without any apparatus, would lack features sufficient for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage across any machinery or no apparatus suggests abstractness and weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: A particular machine or transformation recited in more than general terms can support eligibility if it limits applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular machine or transformation recited in more than general terms may be sufficient to limit the application to just one of several possible machines or changes in state, thereby avoiding preemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with limitations that merely confine use to a technological environment (field-of-use), which may still cover every substantial practical application in that field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations necessary for all practical applications of the natural principle are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional limitations that are necessary for all practical applications of the natural principle (such that everyone practicing the principle would have to perform those steps) would not be sufficient for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed limitations are effectively required for any use of the principle, the claim can improperly preempt the principle and be ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine/Transformation can show integration if it describes how parts implement the natural principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine or transformation can show how the natural principle is integrated into a practical application by describing details of how that machine and its specific parts implement the natural principle or how the transformation relates to/implements the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete description of how components implement the principle supports a finding of practical application (e.g., parts of an internal combustion engine applying combustion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine/transformation that is merely nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related does not show integration
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine or transformation that is merely nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related to the steps (e.g., data gathering or data storage) would not show that these additional features integrate the natural principle into the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a computer used only as an incidental device or a transformation that only changes position/location rather than state/thing does not demonstrate integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete absence of a machine-or-transformation signals likelihood of disembodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete absence of a machine-or-transformation in a claim signals the likelihood that the claim is directed to a natural principle and has not been instantiated (e.g., is disembodied or can be performed entirely in one’s mind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of any machine-or-transformation increases the likelihood the claim is an abstract idea or natural principle without practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere statement of a general concept will effectively monopolize the concept and is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere statement of a general concept (natural principle) would effectively monopolize that concept/principle and would be insufficient for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can be contrasted with a tangible implementation with elements/steps recited with specificity such that all substantial applications are not covered; observable and verifiable steps can provide sufficient specificity.
